records.text: Oh, a fork! One piece jumps to a square that hits several targets at once, and a single reply rarely rescues all of them.
Wait, look at this. One of the other side's pieces now has a jump that forks several targets. Which square is it heading for?
A fork was hiding inside the stronger move, with one piece hitting several targets from a single square. That's the kind of trick worth hunting for every time.
A pin! The piece in front can't step off the line, because its own king is standing behind it on that line.
Hmm, there's a pin coming. After this move, a piece in front of its king can get stuck there, and stepping off the line wouldn't be legal.
The stronger move had a pin that would have kept an enemy piece stuck in front of its king like glue. Here that piece stays free to wander around.
Skewer! The big piece in front has to get out of the way, and then the piece behind it is up for grabs.
Look at this line. Two pieces are stacked on it, just right for a skewer by the other side, which wins whatever stands in back once the front piece moves.
Ooh, a skewer was waiting inside the stronger move! Hit the front piece, it steps aside, grab the one behind. Such a fun pattern.
Knock out the defender first, and the piece it was guarding has nobody watching it anymore. That's the whole trick.
Hmm, a defender can get captured now, and then the piece it was guarding loses its help. Which piece is counting on it?
The stronger move knocked out a defender first, so the piece behind it had nobody watching it. That's a clever move order.
The back rank. The king is boxed in by its own pieces, so that last row is a real weak spot.
See that back rank? After this move the king can't get off it, and the other side has a mate along that row.
The enemy king was stuck on its back row behind its own pieces, and there was mate right there. Set it up and play the mate yourself, it's really cool.
The pawn marches one more step toward promoting. Count the squares: the defenders have less time to stop it now.
An enemy pawn now has a clearer path to promoting. Each step it takes needs an answer from here on.
The stronger move kept a pawn racing toward promoting. This one leaves it sitting still, so the race looks different.
Discovered attack! The front piece slides off, and boom, the piece hiding behind it is suddenly attacking down the line.
Look at this line. One enemy piece is hiding behind another, so when the front piece steps off, the hidden one gets to attack.
A discovered attack was sitting inside the stronger move: slide one piece off the line, and the hidden one behind it strikes. Here that line stays shut.
Ooh, a double attack, two targets hit at the same moment! A single reply rarely covers both of them.
Ooh, see the double attack? After this, the other side gets one move that makes two threats together.
Two threats in one go were waiting in the stronger move. This one doesn't, and that's the difference.
Deflection! The defender gets dragged away to handle something else, and whatever it was guarding is left with no one.
Look, there's a defender here that can be lured away from what it's guarding. What job is it doing right now?
The stronger move tempted a defender off its spot. Set it up and watch everything it was holding fall apart once it leaves.
Free piece! Nothing was guarding it, so it comes off the board without costing anything.
An unguarded enemy piece was sitting there for the stronger move to grab. Always peek for loose pieces before a quiet move.
Look, one piece has nothing guarding it now, and the other side is free to just take it.
Wait, look at this. That piece was the only real guard of another piece, and now it's walked away, so the other piece can be taken.
The opponent's last move made a threat, and this reply doesn't stop it. So a piece can still be captured.
Count the trade all the way to the end. The recapture gets back more than was taken, so the swap loses material.

Passed pawn. No enemy pawn stands in front of it on its file or the files right beside it, so no pawn can block or capture it.

With another move, some piece would have been left with no defender, though that alone wouldn't mean losing it.
The king gets one more square it can step to. A little extra room.
Another move would have handed the king an extra empty square nearby to use.
Castling. The king slides two squares over, and the rook jumps across to stand right next to it.

Doubled pawns: two pawns of the same color now stand one behind the other on a single file.

In the checks and captures, look for one piece that can land on two big targets at once.
Before a pinned piece moves, peek behind it. What's back there, the king or a bigger piece?
Peek past the first target, because something worth more might be lined up behind it.
Before trading off a defender, look at what it was keeping safe.
If a piece leaves a line, look at what that line hits next.
Look for single moves that make two threats, including checks and lines that just opened.
Before a back-row defender walks away, make sure the king still has a square to run to.

Before a defender moves, see which pieces are counting on it.
Before you capture, compare what you take with what the recapture takes back.
When a defender is busy guarding two things, look for a forcing trade that drags it off one of them.
